239.title: Praying with imagination
239.hook: Ignatius puts you inside a gospel scene: the sounds, the dust, where you stand
239.howItsDone: In Ignatian retreats Catholics pray through Gospel scenes one by one, imagining the setting with all the senses, and the wedding at Cana is the second Luminous Mystery of the rosary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, consolation and desolation: movements toward God and away. Your line was notice the pull. Which way were you pulled? Today, one more gift from Ignatius, and it uses the part of you that daydreams. Day two hundred thirty-nine.

Worry is a kind of imagination. So is replaying an old argument in the shower, every line of it, word for word, in a room that's miles away. The mind is very good at putting a person somewhere they aren't. Ignatius's Spiritual Exercises turn that same power toward prayer. Not to invent things about Jesus. To step inside the scenes the Gospels already give, with their sounds and their dust, and find a place to stand. Today the scene is a wedding, and the wine is about to run out.
screen: `WORRY IS IMAGINATION TOO.` → `THE SAME POWER, TURNED TO PRAYER.` → `TODAY: A WEDDING.`

segments.voice: First, the place. Ignatius begins with what he calls composing the place: seeing the setting with the eyes of the imagination. How big is the room? Is it hot? Where are the doors? Second, the senses. He says to apply each sense in turn. What do you see? Who's there? What do you hear, what do they say? What do you smell and taste? What can you touch? You're not making up a new story. You're filling in the one you've been given, the way you'd picture a story a grandparent told you. Third, where you stand. Ignatius asks you to find yourself in the scene. Are you a guest? A servant? Standing near Jesus, or far away? Let's try it with John's Gospel, the wedding at Cana. A wedding in Cana of Galilee. Jesus is there with his disciples, and his mother, Mary. And the wine runs out. Mary says to Jesus, in the Douay-Rheims: "They have no wine." He answers, "Woman, what is that to me and to thee? my hour is not yet come." And she turns to the servants anyway: "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." He tells them to fill six stone water jars, the big ones, to the brim. Then draw some out and carry it to the steward. Fourth, what happens to you. The steward tastes it, calls the groom, and says, "thou hast kept the good wine until now." John calls it the beginning of his miracles. In imaginative prayer the question is: where were you standing when that happened? What did you feel? Catholics say God can speak through what surfaces there.
screen: `COMPOSE THE PLACE.` · `SEE, HEAR, SMELL, TASTE, TOUCH.` · `WHERE DO YOU STAND?` · `CANA: THE WINE RUNS OUT.` · then, large: `WHATSOEVER HE SHALL SAY TO YOU, DO YE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: place yourself in the Cana wedding. Close your eyes and breathe. See the courtyard. Lamps, music, children underfoot, the smell of roasting meat. Now the whisper spreads: the wine is gone. Where are you? Maybe you're a servant, hauling heavy jars of water from the well, arms aching. Maybe you're a guest. Watch Mary lean toward her son. Watch the water poured out. Taste it. Stay wherever you ended up. If you pray, you can speak to Jesus or to Mary there. The bell holds the time.
Praying with imagination. Ignatius's way of stepping inside a Gospel scene with all your senses, and noticing where you stand. Today's word.
Your line: step into the story. Today, when you hear any story, from a friend, a coworker, the news, picture where they were standing before you answer. Day two hundred thirty-nine.

240.title: The Church's clock
240.hook: psalms prayed at set hours around the world by priests, religious and laypeople
240.howItsDone: Catholic priests, deacons and many religious pray the Liturgy of the Hours daily, and laypeople pray morning and evening prayer from a breviary or an app, alone or in parishes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, praying with imagination: stepping into Cana with all your senses. Your line was step into the story. Whose story did you step into? Today, not a scene but a clock, one that has been ticking a very long time. Day two hundred forty.

Right now, as you listen, somewhere on earth it's early morning, and in a monastery chapel a few sleepy monks are standing up to sing a psalm. Somewhere else it's evening, and a parish priest is opening a worn book at his kitchen table. Somewhere else a nurse on a night shift is reading the same psalm on her phone during her break. They've never met. They're praying the same words, set for the same day, on the same clock. The Church has a name for that clock. It's today's word.
screen: `A MONASTERY AT DAWN.` → `A PRIEST AT HIS KITCHEN TABLE.` → `A NURSE ON HER BREAK.`

segments.voice: First, the roots. Praying at set times of day is older than Christianity. The psalmist says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Seven times a day I have given praise to thee." The book of Daniel describes him praying three times a day toward Jerusalem. The Acts of the Apostles tells of Peter and John going up to the Temple at the ninth hour of prayer. The apostles kept the rhythm. Second, the monks. Saint Benedict's Rule organizes the monks' day around these hours, and sets out the whole psalter, all one hundred fifty psalms, every week. Benedict called it the work of God. Nothing, he said, was to be put before it. Over time it came to be prayed above all by monks, nuns and clergy, and it was called the Divine Office. Third, the hours today. After the Second Vatican Council, it was reshaped and published under the title Liturgy of the Hours, though many still call it the Divine Office, and the Church urged laypeople to pray it too, especially morning and evening prayer. The main hours are the Office of Readings, Morning Prayer, Daytime Prayer, Evening Prayer, and Night Prayer, which we'll meet tomorrow. Priests and deacons promise to pray it every day, and religious communities pray it too. Each hour is mostly psalms, a short reading, a hymn and prayers. Fourth, the clock. Because the Church spans every time zone, as one place finishes evening prayer another is beginning morning prayer. The idea is that the whole Church, together, keeps the day holy, hour by hour. Catholics say no one prays it alone, even when they're alone. That's why your line is someone is always praying.
screen: `SEVEN TIMES A DAY: OLDER THAN THE CHURCH.` · `BENEDICT: THE WORK OF GOD.` · `MORNING, DAY, EVENING, NIGHT.` · `EVERY TIME ZONE, ONE PRAYER.` · then, large: `SEVEN TIMES A DAY I HAVE GIVEN PRAISE TO THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray one psalm at sunset, or sit with one. For now, settle and breathe, and here's a line from Psalm 140 that evening prayer uses: let my prayer be directed as incense in thy sight; the lifting up of my hands, as evening sacrifice. Picture the smoke of incense rising in a dark church. Picture hands lifted. Tonight at sunset, find that psalm, or any psalm, and read it slowly. If you pray, pray it. If you don't, read it knowing others are reading it too. The bell holds the time.
Liturgy of the Hours. The Church's daily prayer of psalms at set times, morning to night, prayed around the world. Today's word.
Your line: someone is always praying. Today, when you feel alone, remember the clock: somewhere, right now, someone is praying a psalm. Day two hundred forty.

241.title: Night prayer
241.hook: the short prayer before sleep, with the Nunc Dimittis of Simeon
241.carry: now let your servant go in peace
241.howItsDone: Monks and nuns pray Compline together before the night silence, and other Catholics pray it alone from a breviary or an app; it includes an examination of conscience, psalms, a short reading, the Nunc Dimittis and a closing antiphon to Mary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Liturgy of the Hours, the Church's clock of psalms. Your line was someone is always praying. Did you picture them, somewhere, at your sunset? Today, the last hour of that clock. Day two hundred forty-one.

The lights go down in a monastery chapel. The day's work is over, the last guests have gone, and the monks file in for one more short hour of prayer before bed. It's gentle, almost a lullaby: a look back over the day, a psalm about resting under God's wings, a few lines of reading. And it ends with a man in the Temple, holding a baby, saying he can go in peace. Then the lights go out, and nobody speaks until morning. Today's word is that last hour.
screen: `LIGHTS DOWN IN THE CHAPEL.` → `A SHORT, GENTLE HOUR.` → `A MAN HOLDING A BABY.`

segments.voice: Compline comes from the Latin completorium, the completing. It's the hour that finishes the day. First, the shape. It begins by looking back. In today's Liturgy of the Hours there's a short examination of conscience: what did today hold, what do I regret, what am I grateful for. Then a psalm or two; on Sundays, Psalm 90 in the Douay numbering, the psalm about resting in the shadow of the Most High. Then a short reading, and a response taken from the psalms: into thy hands I commend my spirit. In Luke, Jesus says that line on the cross. Said at bedtime, the echo is hard to miss. Second, the song. The heart of Compline is the canticle of Simeon, from Luke's Gospel. Mary and Joseph bring the infant Jesus to the Temple. A just and devout man named Simeon had been promised he wouldn't die before he saw the Christ. He takes the baby in his arms and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace; because my eyes have seen thy salvation." In Latin it begins Nunc dimittis, now you dismiss, and that's its name. Third, why at night. Simeon is ready to let go. He's seen what he waited for, and he can rest. The Church sets his words at the edge of sleep, a small daily practice of letting go. Fourth, the close. Compline ends with a hymn to Mary, often the Salve Regina, and then the house keeps silence until morning.
screen: `COMPLETORIUM: THE COMPLETING.` · `LOOK BACK, A PSALM, INTO THY HANDS.` · `SIMEON HOLDS THE CHILD.` · `A DAILY PRACTICE OF LETTING GO.` · then, large: `NOW THOU DOST DISMISS THY SERVANT, O LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: end a day the way Compline does. Settle and breathe. Look back over today, quickly and kindly. One thing you regret. One thing you're grateful for. Then, if you pray, you can say Simeon's words slowly: Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace. If you don't pray, just picture Simeon handing the baby back, and let your own day be handed back too. The bell holds the time.
Compline. From the Latin for completing: the last hour of the Church's day, prayed before sleep, with the song of Simeon at its heart. Today's word.
Your line: now let your servant go in peace. Tonight, give the last five minutes before sleep to quiet instead of a screen, and let the day be finished. Day two hundred forty-one.

say nothing, and hand him back.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old word for a bedtime prayer.
what it means: completorium, the completing. the last hour of the Church's day, ending with Simeon's song of letting go.

242.title: The Jesus Prayer
242.hook: loved by Eastern Catholic and Orthodox Christians: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me
242.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians and Byzantine-rite Eastern Catholics often pray the Jesus Prayer many times over on a knotted prayer rope, silently and in rhythm with the breath, and many Latin Catholics use it as well.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Compline, the last hour of the day, and Simeon's song. Your line was now let your servant go in peace. Did you give the day's last minutes to quiet? Today, a prayer short enough to breathe. Day two hundred forty-two.
screen: `NOW LET YOUR SERVANT GO IN PEACE.`

segments.voice: Somewhere in Russia in the 1800s, a man with a knapsack walks from town to town. He's heard a line from Saint Paul read in church, pray without ceasing, and it won't leave him alone. How can anyone pray without stopping? You have to eat. You have to sleep. He asks priest after priest. Finally an old monk hands him one short sentence and tells him to say it, and keep saying it, until it says itself. That's the story in a small anonymous book called The Way of a Pilgrim. Nobody knows who wrote it. But the sentence he's given is real, and it's very old. Today's word is that sentence.
screen: `A PILGRIM WITH A KNAPSACK.` → `PRAY WITHOUT CEASING. BUT HOW?` → `ONE SHORT SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in its common form: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. Many add, a sinner. That's the Jesus Prayer. First, where the words come from. They're stitched out of the Gospels. A blind beggar named Bartimaeus sits by the road outside Jericho, hears Jesus passing, and shouts, in the Douay-Rheims: "Jesus son of David, have mercy on me." People tell him to be quiet. He shouts louder. In another story, a tax collector stands at the back of the Temple and won't even lift his eyes: "O God, be merciful to me a sinner." The Jesus Prayer is those two voices, joined. Second, the name. At its center is the name of Jesus itself. For the Christians who pray it, calling the name is already a way of standing in his presence. Third, the breath. Monks in the Christian East, especially on Mount Athos in Greece, learned to pray it slowly, in rhythm with breathing. Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, on the breath in. Have mercy on me, on the breath out. Their way of stillness is called hesychasm, from a Greek word for quiet. Fourth, who prays it. It's most loved by Orthodox Christians and by Eastern Catholics of the Byzantine tradition, such as Ukrainian and Melkite Greek Catholics. But the Catechism of the Catholic Church describes it and commends it too, so Latin Catholics pray it as well. And have mercy here doesn't mean cringing. It's the same cry as Kyrie eleison at Mass: be kind to me, hold me, heal me.
screen: `BARTIMAEUS AND THE TAX COLLECTOR.` · `THE NAME AT THE CENTER.` · `ONE HALF IN, ONE HALF OUT.` · `EAST AND WEST BOTH PRAY IT.` · then, large: `LORD JESUS CHRIST, SON OF GOD, HAVE MERCY ON ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: breathe it ten times. Settle and let your breath slow. If you pray, breathe in on Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, and breathe out on have mercy on me. Ten times, no hurry. If your mind wanders, just start the next one. If you don't pray, you can breathe in and out on one word, mercy, and notice what it does to your shoulders. The bell holds the time.
The Jesus Prayer. Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me: a Gospel cry, prayed on the breath, loved in the Christian East. Today's word.
Your line: with every breath. Today, when you're waiting, in line, at a red light, for a kettle, try the prayer or the word mercy on three slow breaths. Day two hundred forty-two.

243.title: The kitchen friar (Brother Lawrence, 17th century)
243.hook: a Carmelite lay brother who found God among the pots and pans
243.howItsDone: Catholics and other Christians who read Brother Lawrence's The Practice of the Presence of God try to keep a simple, running conversation with God through ordinary work, especially housework and repetitive tasks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Jesus Prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. Your line was with every breath. Did you find a red light or a kettle to pray on? Today, a man who prayed over a frying pan. Day two hundred forty-three.

A friary kitchen in Paris, in the 1600s. Steam, noise, pots on the boil, people wanting bread and soup at the same time. In the middle of it, a big, clumsy man with a bad leg, an old soldier, who by his own account had a natural dislike of kitchen work. He wasn't a priest. He never wrote a book. He was a lay brother, which meant he did the chores. And yet a priest who came to talk with him about prayer went away and wrote the conversations down. Today's word is that man.
screen: `A LOUD KITCHEN IN PARIS.` → `AN OLD SOLDIER WHO HATED COOKING.` → `A PRIEST WRITES DOWN HIS WORDS.`

segments.voice: His name was Nicholas Herman, and in the Carmelite order he became Brother Lawrence of the Resurrection. First, how it began. As a young man, before he joined, he looked at a bare tree in winter. No leaves, no fruit. And it struck him that in a few months it would be green and heavy with fruit again. He said later that this moment gave him a sense of God's care that never left him. A tree in winter. That's all it took. Second, the kitchen. He was put to work cooking, and he says he had a natural dislike of it. So he made a choice. He would do every small task for the love of God. He talks about turning a cake in the pan, or picking up a straw from the floor, as a way of loving God. Nothing had to be grand. Third, the method, if you can call it that. He called it the practice of the presence of God: talking to God simply, all day, in the middle of whatever he was doing. Not waiting for chapel. He said the time of work and the time of prayer were no different for him, and that in the noise of the kitchen he felt as calm as if he were kneeling before the Blessed Sacrament. Fourth, how we know. He wrote very little. After he died, that priest gathered the conversations and a handful of letters into a small book, The Practice of the Presence of God. It's short enough to read in an evening, and small enough for a coat pocket.
screen: `A BARE TREE IN WINTER.` · `EVERY SMALL TASK FOR LOVE.` · `THE PRACTICE OF THE PRESENCE.` · `A SMALL BOOK, GATHERED AFTER.` · then, large: `THE TIME OF WORK IS THE TIME OF PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wash dishes as prayer. If there's a sink nearby, go to it. If not, do it later and use this time to picture it. Warm water. One plate at a time. Don't rush to be done. If you pray, you can talk to God the way Brother Lawrence did, plainly, as if God were standing at the counter beside you. If you don't, just give the plate your whole attention, and let it be enough. The bell holds the time.
The kitchen friar. Brother Lawrence, a Carmelite lay brother in seventeenth-century Paris, who practiced God's presence among the pots and pans. Today's word.
Your line: god among the pots. Today, pick one chore you dislike and do it slowly, on purpose, for love of God or for love of someone. Day two hundred forty-three.

244.title: Centering prayer
244.hook: a quiet method from Trappist monks in the 1970s, rooted in older teaching
244.howItsDone: People who practice centering prayer usually sit for about twenty minutes, often twice a day, using a chosen sacred word as a sign of consent to God, and some join small groups that sit together in parishes and retreat houses.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the kitchen friar, Brother Lawrence, praying over the pots. Your line was god among the pots. Which chore did you do slowly, on purpose? Today, a prayer with almost no words at all. Day two hundred forty-four.

Massachusetts, the early 1970s. Young people are knocking at a Trappist monastery, and some of them are on their way to Eastern teachers of meditation. The monks notice. Some of those young people were raised Catholic, and say they never heard that their own Church had a tradition of silent prayer. The abbot asks a question: could we put that old tradition into a simple form, something a busy person could actually do? Three monks, the abbot among them, get to work. Today's word is what they came up with.
screen: `A MONASTERY IN MASSACHUSETTS.` → `WHERE IS OUR OWN SILENCE?` → `A SIMPLE FORM FOR BUSY PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: The monastery was Saint Joseph's Abbey in Spencer, Massachusetts. The abbot was Thomas Keating, and with him were William Meninger and Basil Pennington. They called it centering prayer. First, the roots. They didn't invent the silence. They drew on the desert fathers, on an old English book we'll meet tomorrow, and on Jesus's own words in the Sermon on the Mount. In the Douay-Rheims: "But thou when thou shalt pray, enter into thy chamber, and having shut the door, pray to thy Father in secret." The inner room. Second, the method. You choose a sacred word, short and simple: God, Jesus, Abba, peace, love. The word isn't a mantra you repeat over and over. It's a sign of your intention. You sit comfortably, eyes closed, and introduce the word gently. That's it. Third, the thoughts. They will come. Plans, worries, the grocery list. The teaching is not to fight them. When you notice you're caught up in one, you return, ever so gently, to the sacred word. In this method, every return counts as a small yes. Fourth, what it's for. Not a special experience. Not emptying the mind. Its founders describe it as consenting to God's presence and action within, trusting that something is happening even when it feels like nothing. Catholics don't all agree about it. Some parishes and retreat houses teach it. Some Catholic writers are more cautious, and prefer prayer with more words and images. Both sit inside the Church.
screen: `THREE MONKS, AN OLD TRADITION.` · `CHOOSE A SACRED WORD.` · `RETURN, EVER SO GENTLY.` · `CONSENT, NOT A FEELING.` · then, large: `ENTER INTO THY CHAMBER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose a sacred word and sit. Pick one short word now. If you pray, it might be God, or Jesus, or Abba. If you don't, try peace, or yes. Close your eyes. Let the word arrive once, softly, as a sign that you're willing to be here. Then let it go. When you notice you're thinking, don't scold yourself. Just come back to the word, gently. The bell holds the time.
Centering prayer. A simple method of silent prayer from Trappist monks in the 1970s: one sacred word, and a gentle return, as consent to God's presence. Today's word.
Your line: consent to his presence. Today, when your mind runs away, come back without scolding it, the way you'd call back a dog that wandered. Day two hundred forty-four.

245.title: The Cloud of Unknowing (14th century)
245.hook: an anonymous English guide: God is reached by love, not by thinking
245.howItsDone: Some Catholics read The Cloud of Unknowing as a guide to silent, wordless prayer, repeating a single short word like God or love as a movement of the heart, and it underlies modern methods such as centering prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, centering prayer: one sacred word and a gentle return. Your line was consent to his presence. Did you call your mind back without scolding it? Today, the old book those monks leaned on. Day two hundred forty-five.

A swimming manual has never kept anyone afloat. A list of reasons to love someone is not the love. Some things can't be reached by thinking. Somewhere in England, in the 1300s, a writer whose name we'll never know sat down to teach a young person how to pray, and made exactly this point about God. The book is short, strange, and funny in places. Its title is today's word.
screen: `YOU CAN'T THINK YOUR WAY INTO LOVE.` → `ENGLAND, THE 1300S.` → `A WRITER WITH NO NAME.`

segments.voice: The Cloud of Unknowing was written in Middle English, the English of Chaucer's time, by an author who hid his name on purpose. Some readers guess he was a priest, perhaps a Carthusian monk. Nobody knows. First, the two clouds. When you turn toward God, he says, you find a darkness between you and God, a cloud of unknowing. Your mind can't get through it. So you put everything else, all your thoughts, even good ones, beneath you in a cloud of forgetting. Second, the key. God can't be reached by thinking, he says, but God can be reached by love. He puts it in a line of two halves: by love God may be gotten and held, but by thought never. Your mind can know about God. Only love can touch God. Third, the dart. So what do you do in the cloud? You send up what he calls a sharp dart of longing love. Keep it short. He suggests one word, even one syllable, like God, or love, and says to fasten it to your heart. A short prayer, he says, pierces heaven. His own picture: someone whose house is on fire doesn't make a speech. They shout one word, fire. Fourth, the humor. He warns against people who strain so hard at prayer that they pull strange faces and twist themselves about. Relax, he says. Don't force it. Our last two weeks have walked through ways of praying: contemplation, lectio divina, the examen, imagination, the Hours, Compline, the Jesus Prayer, a kitchen, a sacred word, and now a cloud. Tomorrow, a saint builds a castle.
screen: `A CLOUD OF UNKNOWING ABOVE.` · `BY LOVE, NOT BY THOUGHT.` · `A SHARP DART OF LONGING LOVE.` · `DON'T STRAIN. DON'T FORCE IT.` · then, large: `SHORT PRAYER PIERCES HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: send a short dart of love. Settle. Let your thoughts drift down beneath you, even the good ones. If you pray, choose one word, God or love, and send it upward, short and whole, whenever you feel the pull. No explaining. If you don't pray, send the word toward whatever you love most, and let the word do the loving. The bell holds the time.
The Cloud of Unknowing. An anonymous English guide from the 1300s: God can't be held by thinking, only by love. Today's word.

Your line: by love, not thought. Today, when you catch yourself overthinking someone you love, stop analyzing and do one kind thing for them instead. Day two hundred forty-five. Two weeks of ways of praying, done.

the book says God can be reached by love, not by thought
the mind can know about God; only love can touch God.

fork.setup: you're sitting in prayer, and all you find is darkness, a cloud your mind can't get through. what does the book say to do?
options: think harder until you understand.
give up; this prayer isn't for you.
send up a short dart of longing love.
fork.reveal: love, not thought, gets through the cloud. keep it short: one word, even one syllable.

trapdoor: what you thought: a mystical book with a spooky title.
what it means: a practical guide: God is beyond the mind, so you reach God by short, whole acts of love.
what a scholar hears: Middle English, 14th century, anonymous; it draws on the tradition of Pseudo-Dionysius, who taught that God is known in darkness.
